title: Molecular Basis of Inheritance
subject: Biology
subtitle: Class 12 HSC & MHT-CET • Rapid Revision Deck

cards.q: Frederick Griffith's Transformation Experiment (1928) on Streptococcus pneumoniae?
cards.a:
Used two strains:
- S-strain (Smooth): Virulent, encapsulated with mucous polysaccharide coat; kills mice.
- R-strain (Rough): Non-virulent, non-capsulated; mice survive.
Observations:
1. Heat-killed S-strain $\rightarrow$ Mice live.
2. Heat-killed S-strain + Live R-strain $\rightarrow$ Mice DIE (live virulent S-strain recovered).
Conclusion: A 'Transforming Principle' transferred from dead S-strain transformed live R-strain into virulent S-strain.
cards.hint: Griffith proved genetic transformation occurred, but did NOT identify the biochemical nature of the transforming agent.

cards.q: Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty Experiment (1944): Biochemical characterization?
cards.a:
Purified biochemical components (proteins, RNA, DNA) from heat-killed S cells:
1. Protease + Heat-killed S + Live R $\rightarrow$ Transformation occurred.
2. RNase + Heat-killed S + Live R $\rightarrow$ Transformation occurred.
3. DNase + Heat-killed S + Live R $\rightarrow$ Transformation INHIBITED.
Conclusion: DNA is the transforming principle (the hereditary material).
cards.hint: DNase specifically digested DNA and destroyed the transforming activity, proving DNA is genetic.

cards.q: Hershey-Chase (1952) Blender Experiment: Unequivocal proof of DNA as genetic material?
cards.a:
Used Bacteriophage T2 and E. coli:
1. Phage labeled with $^{35}S$ (labeled protein coat, since sulfur is in methionine/cysteine).
2. Phage labeled with $^{32}P$ (labeled DNA core, since phosphorus is in nucleic acids).
Steps: Infection $\rightarrow$ Blending (sheared coats) $\rightarrow$ Centrifugation.
Results:
- Supernatant contained $^{35}S$ (protein coats remained outside).
- Pellet (bacteria) contained $^{32}P$ (DNA entered bacterial cells).
Conclusion: DNA, not protein, is the genetic material.
cards.hint: Unequivocal, universally accepted proof that DNA is the genetic material.

cards.q: Chargaff's Rules of DNA Base Equivalence?
cards.a:
Applies strictly to double-stranded DNA (dsDNA):
1. Purines = Pyrimidines: $[A] + [G] = [C] + [T]$.
2. Amount of Adenine = Thymine: $[A] / [T] = 1$.
3. Amount of Guanine = Cytosine: $[G] / [C] = 1$.
4. Base ratio $(A + T) / (G + C)$ is constant for a given species, but varies between species.
cards.hint: If a dsDNA has 20% Cytosine, then Guanine = 20%, total G+C = 40%, so A+T = 60%, meaning Adenine = 30% and Thymine = 30%.

cards.q: Salient features of Watson-Crick B-DNA Double Helix Model?
cards.a:
1. Two antiparallel polynucleotide chains ($5' \rightarrow 3'$ and $3' \rightarrow 5'$).
2. Sugar-phosphate backbone outside; bases project inside paired via H-bonds: A=T (2 H-bonds) and G≡C (3 H-bonds).
3. Pitch of helix = 3.4 nm (34 Å) with ~10 base pairs per turn.
4. Distance between consecutive base pairs = 0.34 nm (3.4 Å).
5. Diameter of double helix = 2.0 nm (20 Å).
cards.hint: Right-handed coiled B-DNA is the predominant physiological form.

cards.q: Packaging of DNA in Eukaryotes: Structure of a Nucleosome?
cards.a:
Proposed by Roger Kornberg (1974):
- Histone Octamer core (2 molecules each of $H_2A, H_2B, H_3, H_4$; rich in basic amino acids Lysine and Arginine).
- Negatively charged DNA wrapped ~1.75 turns around octamer (~146 base pairs).
- $H_1$ histone seals the entry/exit point of DNA (linker DNA has ~54 bp).
- Total DNA per nucleosome bead = ~200 base pairs.
cards.hint: Under electron microscopy, chromatin appears as 'beads-on-a-string'.

cards.q: Euchromatin vs Heterochromatin: Core differences?
cards.a:
1. Euchromatin: Loosely packed, lightly staining regions; replicates early in S-phase; transcriptionally ACTIVE.
2. Heterochromatin: Densely packed, darkly staining regions (found near centromeres and telomeres); replicates late in S-phase; transcriptionally INACTIVE / silent.
cards.hint: Heterochromatin is transcriptionally inert due to high methylation and tight chromatin compaction.

cards.q: Meselson and Stahl Experiment (1958): Semi-Conservative DNA Replication?
cards.a:
Grew E. coli in $^{15}NH_4Cl$ (heavy isotope) medium for generations $\rightarrow$ all DNA was heavy ($^{15}N/^{15}N$).
Transferred to normal $^{14}NH_4Cl$ medium:
- Generation 1 (after 20 min): 100% Hybrid intermediate density ($^{15}N/^{14}N$).
- Generation 2 (after 40 min): 50% Hybrid ($^{15}N/^{14}N$) and 50% Light ($^{14}N/^{14}N$).
Density measured using CsCl equilibrium density gradient centrifugation.
cards.hint: Taylor (1958) proved semi-conservative replication in eukaryotes using radioactive tritiated thymidine ($^3H$-thymidine) on Vicia faba.

cards.q: Enzymes of DNA Replication and their specific functions?
cards.a:
1. Helicase: Unwinds the double helix by breaking H-bonds at Ori.
2. Topoisomerase (DNA Gyrase): Relieves supercoiling and torsional strain ahead of replication fork.
3. SSBP: Prevents single strands from re-annealing.
4. RNA Primase: Synthesizes short RNA primer (5-10 nt) providing free 3'-OH group.
5. DNA Polymerase III: Synthesizes new DNA strand in strictly $5' \rightarrow 3'$ direction.
6. DNA Polymerase I: Removes RNA primer (5'->3' exonuclease) and fills gaps.
7. DNA Ligase: Joins Okazaki fragments via phosphodiester bonds.
cards.hint: DNA polymerase cannot initiate synthesis de novo; it strictly requires a free 3'-OH primer.

cards.q: Leading Strand vs Lagging Strand synthesis at the Replication Fork?
cards.a:
1. Leading Strand: Synthesized continuously towards the replication fork on the $3' \rightarrow 5'$ template strand; requires only 1 RNA primer.
2. Lagging Strand: Synthesized discontinuously away from the replication fork on the $5' \rightarrow 3'$ template strand as short Okazaki fragments (1000-2000 nt in prokaryotes); requires multiple RNA primers.
cards.hint: Okazaki fragments are joined into a continuous strand by DNA Ligase.

cards.q: Structure of a Transcription Unit: Promoter, Structural Gene, Terminator?
cards.a:
1. Promoter: DNA sequence located upstream at 5'-end (with respect to coding strand) where RNA polymerase and transcription factors bind (TATA box / Pribnow box).
2. Structural gene: Flanked by promoter and terminator; contains Template strand ($3' \rightarrow 5'$) and Coding strand ($5' \rightarrow 3'$).
3. Terminator: Sequence located downstream at 3'-end where transcription stops.
cards.hint: All reference coordinates (upstream/downstream) in a transcription unit are defined with respect to the CODING strand!

cards.q: Eukaryotic RNA Polymerases and their transcribed products?
cards.a:
1. RNA Polymerase I: Transcribes 28S, 18S, and 5.8S rRNAs.
2. RNA Polymerase II: Transcribes precursor of mRNA, called heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA).
3. RNA Polymerase III: Transcribes tRNA, 5S rRNA, and snRNAs (small nuclear RNAs).
cards.hint: Prokaryotes have only ONE single RNA polymerase that synthesizes all types of RNA.

cards.q: Post-Transcriptional Processing of Eukaryotic hnRNA: Capping, Tailing, Splicing?
cards.a:
1. Capping: Addition of unusual nucleotide 7-methylguanosine triphosphate ($m^7Gppp$) to the 5'-end of hnRNA.
2. Tailing: Addition of Poly-A tail (200-300 adenylate residues) to the 3'-end in a template-independent manner.
3. Splicing: Removal of non-coding intervening sequences (Introns) and joining of coding sequences (Exons) by spliceosome complex (snRNPs).
cards.hint: Split-gene arrangement (presence of introns) is an ancient, diagnostic characteristic of eukaryotes.

cards.q: Key properties of the Genetic Code?
cards.a:
1. Triplet: 3 consecutive nucleotides form a codon ($4^3 = 64$ codons for 20 amino acids).
2. Universal: Codon codes for same amino acid from bacteria to humans (e.g. UUU codes for Phenylalanine).
3. Degenerate: Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon (e.g. Leucine coded by 6 codons).
4. Commaless & Non-overlapping: Read continuously without punctuation.
5. Non-ambiguous & Specific: 1 codon codes for ONLY 1 specific amino acid.
cards.hint: AUG has dual functions: acts as Start/Initiator codon AND codes for Methionine.

cards.q: Start and Stop Codons: Triplet sequences?
cards.a:
Start Codon: AUG (codes for Methionine in eukaryotes; N-formylmethionine in prokaryotes).
Stop (Nonsense / Termination) Codons:
1. UAA (Ochre)
2. UAG (Amber)
3. UGA (Opal)
These 3 codons do not code for any amino acid and have no corresponding tRNAs (recognized by Release Factors).
cards.hint: Out of 64 total codons, exactly 61 are sense codons and 3 are nonsense/stop codons.

cards.q: Structure of tRNA (Transfer RNA): Cloverleaf vs L-shaped model?
cards.a:
Secondary structure is Cloverleaf model (Robert Holley); Tertiary structure is compact 3D inverted L-shape (Kim & Klug).
Key arms:
1. Acceptor stem: 3'-end with CCA-OH sequence where specific amino acid binds.
2. Anticodon loop: Contains 3 bases complementary to mRNA codon.
3. D-loop (DHU loop): Binds Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase enzyme.
4. T$\psi$C loop: Binds ribosome.
cards.hint: Francis Crick termed tRNA the 'Adapter Molecule'.

cards.q: Translation: Activation of Amino Acid and Aminoacylation of tRNA?
cards.a:
1. Activation: Amino acid + ATP $\rightarrow$ Aminoacyl-AMP-Enzyme complex + PPi (catalyzed by Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase in presence of $Mg^{2+}$).
2. Charging (Aminoacylation): Activated amino acid is transferred to the 3'-CCA end of its cognate tRNA, releasing AMP and enzyme:
Aminoacyl-AMP-Enzyme + tRNA $\rightarrow$ Aminoacyl-tRNA (charged tRNA) + AMP + Enzyme.
cards.hint: Charging of tRNA requires ATP energy and ensures fidelity of protein translation.

cards.q: Steps of Translation Elongation: Peptidyl transferase and Translocation?
cards.a:
1. Ribosome sites: A-site (Aminoacyl/entry), P-site (Peptidyl/peptidyl-tRNA), E-site (Exit).
2. Peptide bond formation: Catalyzed by Peptidyl transferase (in bacteria, the 23S rRNA acts as a ribozyme) between amino acid on P-site and A-site.
3. Translocation: Ribosome shifts 1 codon along mRNA ($5' \rightarrow 3'$) via Elongation Factor G (EF-G) and GTP, moving uncharged tRNA to E-site.
cards.hint: 23S rRNA in prokaryotes is a ribozyme (RNA acting as an enzyme).

cards.q: Lac Operon: Structure and components (Jacob & Monod, 1961)?
cards.a:
Inducible catabolic operon in E. coli:
1. Regulatory gene ($i$ gene): Constitutively synthesizes Lac Repressor protein.
2. Promoter ($P$): Binding site for RNA polymerase.
3. Operator ($O$): Binding site for active repressor protein.
4. Structural genes:
- $lacZ$: Codes for $\beta$-galactosidase (hydrolyzes lactose into glucose + galactose).
- $lacY$: Codes for $\beta$-galactoside Permease (increases cell permeability to lactose).
- $lacA$: Codes for $\beta$-galactoside Transacetylase.
cards.hint: All three structural genes are transcribed as a single polycistronic mRNA in prokaryotes.

cards.q: Lac Operon Regulation: Switched OFF vs Switched ON mechanism?
cards.a:
1. In ABSENCE of Inducer (Lactose):
Repressor protein binds tightly to Operator ($O$) site $\rightarrow$ blocks RNA polymerase from transcribing structural genes $\rightarrow$ Operon is OFF (no enzymes synthesized).
2. In PRESENCE of Inducer (Allolactose/Lactose):
Inducer binds to repressor protein causing conformational change (inactivating it) $\rightarrow$ Repressor cannot bind to operator $\rightarrow$ RNA polymerase transcribes $lacZ, lacY, lacA$ $\rightarrow$ Operon is ON.
cards.hint: Lac operon is under NEGATIVE INDUCIBLE control (repressor prevents transcription unless inactivated by inducer).

cards.q: Human Genome Project (HGP): Key goals and methodologies?
cards.a:
13-year mega-project (1990-2003) coordinated by US DOE and NIH, Wellcome Trust.
Goals: Sequence all 3 billion base pairs of human DNA, identify all ~20,000-25,000 genes, store data in bioinformatics databases.
Methodologies:
1. ESTs (Expressed Sequence Tags): Identifying all genes expressed as RNA.
2. Sequence Annotation: Sequencing blind entire genome and assigning functions later using BAC and YAC vectors and automated Sanger sequencers.
cards.hint: Chromosome 1 was the last chromosome to be completely sequenced (completed May 2006).

cards.q: Salient findings of the Human Genome Project?
cards.a:
1. Human genome contains 3.1647 billion base pairs (3164.7 Mb).
2. Average gene contains 3000 bases; largest human gene is Dystrophin on X chromosome (2.4 million bases).
3. Total estimated genes = ~25,000 (much fewer than earlier expected ~100,000).
4. Less than 2% of the genome codes for proteins.
5. Over 50% discovered genes have unknown functions.
6. Repeated sequences make up very large portion of genome.
7. ~1.4 million locations have single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).
cards.hint: Any two individuals share 99.9% identical nucleotide base sequences (only 0.1% accounts for all phenotypic variation).

cards.q: DNA Fingerprinting: Principle and VNTRs (Sir Alec Jeffreys)?
cards.a:
Technique developed by Sir Alec Jeffreys (1984); Dr. Lalji Singh and Dr. V.K. Kashyap pioneered it in India.
Principle: Based on DNA polymorphism in non-coding satellite DNA (repetitive DNA).
Uses VNTRs (Variable Number of Tandem Repeats / Minisatellites: 11-60 bp repeats) which show high degree of individual polymorphism and are inherited from parents.
cards.hint: Monozygotic (identical) twins have 100% identical DNA fingerprints.

cards.q: Steps of DNA Fingerprinting Protocol?
cards.a:
1. DNA Isolation: Extraction from blood, semen, hair root, saliva.
2. Restriction Digestion: DNA cut into fragments by restriction endonuclease.
3. Agarose Gel Electrophoresis: Separation of fragments based on size.
4. Southern Blotting: Denaturation and transfer of separated DNA fragments from gel to nitrocellulose/nylon membrane.
5. Hybridization: Incubation with radiolabeled radioactive $^{32}P$-VNTR probes.
6. Autoradiography: Visualization of hybrid bands on X-ray film.
cards.hint: Southern blotting transfers DNA; Northern blotting transfers RNA; Western blotting transfers proteins.

cards.q: MHT-CET Numerical Trap: Calculate length of DNA in a human diploid cell.
cards.a:
Total base pairs in human diploid cell = $6.6 \times 10^9$ bp.
Distance between consecutive base pairs = $0.34 \times 10^{-9}$ m.
Total DNA length = $(6.6 \times 10^9) \times (0.34 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m}) \approx 2.24$ metres!
This 2.24 m DNA is packaged into a nucleus of diameter only $\approx 10^{-6}$ m via nucleosomal winding.
cards.hint: E. coli DNA has $4.6 \times 10^6$ bp; its length is $\approx 1.36$ mm.
